Take ArguAna: interpolation makes 19.1% of queries worse, the worsened queries drop by 0.213 on average, almost as much as the 0.221 average gain of the improved queries, and the mean net change is only +0.0077. The small rise in the average is the difference left after large gains and large losses across many queries cancel out.

One might suspect that the 0.7 weight was picked on the test data. The authors re-select the weight with leave-one-dataset-out cross-validation: choose α on the other 6 datasets and apply it to the 7th. The resulting deployable tax is 11–25%, slightly higher than with a fixed 0.7, which shows the tax is not caused by tuning on the test set. The risk-sensitive test TRisk, which weights the losses of worsened queries more heavily, judges interpolation riskier than dense-only retrieval on 6 of the 7 datasets.

3.3 Which quadrant the losses come from

This experiment checks which kind of query the losses come from. The authors split interpolation's per-query gains and losses by the four quadrants of Section 2 (paper Table VII). Result: Sparse-Only queries make up no more than 7% of the total, but 87–95% of them are hurt by fusion, with mean net losses of 0.14 to 0.37 within the quadrant. The reason is that dense retrieval has no relevant document in its top 10 on these queries, and the 0.7 dense weight pushes down the relevant documents BM25 found. Dense-Only queries are the mirror case: BM25 becomes the noise source and 38–65% are hurt. Among Both-Win queries, 10–48% are reordered, with help and harm nearly cancelling and a quadrant net change between −0.04 and +0.01; because this quadrant holds the most queries, it contributes 38–72% of the worsened queries.

The losses are mainly rank changes, not lost relevant documents: queries whose top-10 recall drops are only 1–7%, and most of the loss is relevant documents moving down within the top 10; across all datasets, 77 queries have all their relevant documents pushed out of the top 10.

3.4 A bigger encoder does not remove the tax

This experiment checks whether the fusion tax exists only because the dense model is weak. The authors step the dense encoder up from 22M to 596M, then redo the experiment with BM25 replaced by the learned sparse retriever SPLADE. Result: with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, interpolation still puts 14–43% of queries below the per-query best; with SPLADE it is 14–41% on 6 datasets and 60% on TREC-COVID. A stronger encoder only changes the balance between the two retrievers, and that balance decides which retriever becomes noise on each query, so the share of hurt queries does not decline as the encoder grows.

3.5 Can we tell in advance which queries should not be fused

If this could be predicted, queries could be routed: fuse where fusion helps and use dense-only retrieval elsewhere. This experiment checks whether that is feasible. The authors extract 17 features available at inference time for each query (query length, IDF statistics of its terms, the score gap between the first and second result of each retriever, the overlap of the two top-10 lists, and so on) and train gradient-boosted trees to predict whether fusion will fail. Result: AUC is 0.63 within a dataset, falls to 0.59 across datasets, and is as low as 0.49, close to random; 11 of the 17 features flip the direction of their association with failure across datasets. A router built on these features does not beat fixed interpolation on any dataset. A concrete example is the dense side's score lead: on datasets where dense retrieval is stronger it signals that fusion is safe, but on TREC-COVID it signals that fusion will fail.

3.6 Can reranking repair the damage

This experiment checks whether a cross-encoder reranker after fusion can repair the losses fusion causes. The authors rerank the top 30 with BGE-reranker-v2-m3. Result: the deployable tax falls by a third on SciFact and does not fall on FiQA or TREC-COVID. Reranking both repairs losses and creates new ones: on SciFact it repairs 27 of the 30 previously hurt queries and newly hurts 17; on FiQA it repairs 75 of 95 and newly hurts 81; on TREC-COVID it repairs 5 of 7 and newly hurts 9. After reranking, nDCG@10 differs by at most 0.011 whether the candidates come from interpolation or from dense-only retrieval. On cost, BM25 takes 1.1–4.3 ms per query on an Apple M5, while cross-encoder reranking of 30 candidates takes about 1.6 s.

4. Limitations

The authors list five limitations: only retrieval ranking is evaluated, not the final answer generation; only one reranker and one reranking depth are tried; TREC-COVID has only 50 queries, so its percentages fluctuate a lot; latency is measured on one machine only; and the prediction experiment uses only cheap features, without trying LLM judgments.

Two further points deserve attention. First, all 7 datasets are English BEIR datasets whose queries are mostly natural-language questions, and dense retrieval is stronger than BM25 on all 7 of them; in keyword-heavy settings such as e-commerce or code search, Sparse-Only queries may be far more than 7%, and both the quadrant shares and the recommended weight need to be re-measured. Second, Section 3.3 shows that most of the loss is relevant documents moving down within the top 10; if the downstream system feeds all 10 documents into the generator's context, this loss affects the answer much less, which is exactly the gap left by not evaluating generation.

5. Practical implications

First, before adopting hybrid retrieval, measure the nDCG@10 of each retriever on the target corpus. The authors' rule is: if dense retrieval leads by more than 0.04, use score interpolation with a dense weight of 0.6–0.7; if the two are close, use RRF, CombMNZ or interpolation with weight 0.5. Labeling 200–400 queries is enough to make this call, and transferring the 0.6–0.7 weight to another dataset costs at most 0.014.

Second, in online evaluation, report "the share of queries worse than dense-only retrieval" and "the mean loss when worse" alongside the average. These two numbers show directly whether a higher average comes from most queries gaining a little, or from some queries gaining a lot and cancelling out large losses on others.

papers.title: pplx-embed-v2-late Technical Report
papers.authors: Markus Krimmel, Louis Milliken, Ekaterina Glazkova, Maximilian Schall, Antoine Chaffin, Sedigheh Eslami, Jonas Golde, De...
papers.summary: Perplexity releases 0.6B and 9B multi-vector retrievers that encode text, images, and document screenshots: each document token stores a 128-d vector, and scoring sums MaxSim of each query vector against document vectors. Both models distill token-by-token from the same 18B teacher, ==so they share one vector space== and a 9B offline document index can be queried by a 0.6B online encoder. On 72 domain retrieval tasks the 9B model averages nDCG@10 81.3%, 1.6 points above nemotron-3-embed-8b; a 0.6B query with a 9B index scores 79.6%, above 78.0% when both ends use 0.6B. On BrowseComp+ the 9B model lets an agent answer 64.0% correctly with the fewest searches.

deep_reading.content_html:
Perplexity releases two multi-vector retrieval models, pplx-embed-v2-late at 0.6B and 9B, that encode text, images, and document page screenshots. They are late-interaction retrievers: every document token stores a 128-d vector, every query token gets a vector, and scoring sums MaxSim—each query vector takes its max inner product against document vectors. The two models are not trained separately with contrastive learning; they both distill token-by-token from the same 18B teacher's output vectors, so they live in one vector space: the corpus can be indexed offline with 9B and queried online with 0.6B. On the authors' 72 domain retrieval tasks, 9B averages nDCG@10 81.3%, 1.6 points above next-best nemotron-3-embed-8b; a 0.6B query with a 9B index scores 79.6%, 1.6 points above both ends at 0.6B, with unchanged query-side cost. Note that the full list of the 72 tasks is not public, so the scores cannot be independently reproduced.

1. Why late interaction, why distill

Retrievers usually trade off between single-vector ANN (fast, loses detail) and cross-encoders (strong, one pass per candidate, only for reranking). Late interaction sits in between: document token vectors are precomputed; at query time only query vectors are computed, then MaxSim. Storage is the cost, so this work compresses each token vector to 128-d.

The authors' other judgment: small models trained with contrastive learning alone are not strong enough; fitting a large model's token vectors works better. A side effect is that differently sized students distilled from the same teacher are interchangeable.

2. Training

2.1 18B teacher: two-stage contrastive learning

The teacher is Qwen3.5-27B with the last 20 layers dropped (18B) and causal masks removed so every token sees both sides. Training has two stages.

Stage 1 uses query–document pairs from 28 datasets, further split by language and domain into 981 subsets, 186M pairs total (88.3% text–text, 8.3% text–image, 3.4% text–screenshot); sampling weights change the mix to 56.5% / 30.9% / 12.6%. Each batch comes from one subset so in-batch negatives are harder. To hit target mix and even spacing, subsets are sampled with a golden-ratio quasi-random sequence rather than independent draws. Contrastive batch size is 16,384 pairs, LoRA rank 128; MaxSim is a Triton kernel to avoid materializing the token-level similarity matrix.

Stage 2 merges LoRA, adds a new rank-32 adapter, freezes vision, and trains only on text triples: each query with one positive and up to 4 hard negatives. Some hard negatives are synthesized by editing key fields in highly templated documents.

2.2 Students: token-wise fit to teacher vectors

Student loss is direct: for every valid query and document token, Euclidean distance between L2-normalized student and teacher vectors, averaged on the query side and document side then summed. The teacher is frozen.
L=∣Q∣1​(i,t)∈Q∑​∥qitS​−qitT​∥2​+∣D∣1​(i,t)∈D∑​∥ditS​−ditT​∥2​
Because the loss needs no in-batch negatives, a batch can mix subsets and gradients are stabler. The 9B student is based on Qwen3.5-9B; LoRA alone underfit, so the last 8 text layers are fully fine-tuned and the rest use LoRA. The 0.6B student is pruned from Qwen3.5-0.8B by dropping 2 of 3 Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers per block (594M total; 254M embedding, 100M vision; ~240M active on text) and is fully fine-tuned.

3. Experiments

3.1 Text retrieval

This checks whether the two distilled models beat same-size single-vector models on text. The domain suite has 72 public tasks (finance 18, law 20, medical 8, dialogue 5, tech 4, multilingual 17), nDCG@10, equal-weight average over six domains:

9B leads every domain except medical; 0.6B leads every domain among sub-1B models.

Q2D-Web is closer to Perplexity's online setting: ~70K agent-rewritten online search queries over 190M web pages, Recall@1000. Relevance merges three sources: documents the agent actually cited, documents ranked high by the online retriever, and LLM-judged relevant docs. On that merge, 9B and 0.6B score 74.8% and 73.6% versus 69.3% for the strongest baseline nemotron-3-embed-8b. This benchmark comes from Perplexity traffic; other models were not tuned for it.

3.2 Document screenshots and images

On images it is not fully dominant. On ViDoRe-V3, vision-specialized EVIE-8B (66.4%) and EVIE-4.5B (65.9%) are higher, but they store 4,096 and 2,048 dims per token, while pplx-embed-v2-late stores only 128-d. On MIRACL-Vision (Wikipedia screenshots) and PPLX-Q2I (Perplexity online image-search logs: 10K queries, 100K images), gemini-embedding-2 is higher.

3.3 Small-model query + large-model index

This checks whether the shared vector space is usable in deployment. Index documents with 9B; encode queries with 9B or 0.6B. 0.6B query + 9B docs beats both-ends-0.6B in all six domains, averaging 79.6% versus 78.0% (both-ends-9B is 81.3%). Query encoding cost matches pure 0.6B; document index cost is amortized over the index lifetime.

3.4 As the retriever for a search agent

BrowseComp+ lets GPT-OSS-120B act as an agent that repeatedly searches a fixed corpus with the tested retriever and answers complex questions, scored by another LLM. 9B accuracy is 64.0%, 4.9 points above another late-interaction model Reason-ModernColBERT and 8.7 above the best single-vector voyage-4-large; mean search count is also lower than every baseline, and recall is highest.

4. Limitations

No storage or latency numbers are given. Multi-vector indexes store a 128-d vector per token; how much more storage and MaxSim cost that is versus single-vector at web scale is unstated. The domain-task list is private, so scores cannot be reproduced. On image retrieval, specialized vision models and gemini-embedding-2 still win on some benchmarks. The claim that distillation beats pure contrastive learning—especially for small models—has no contrastive numbers in the body.

5. Takeaways

For retrieval teams, the most directly usable piece is "large model indexes, small model queries": document compute is paid once, query latency is 0.6B, and quality beats a pure small model by 1.6 points. The premise is that both ends are distilled from the same teacher; independently trained models cannot be mixed this way. The 0.6B text side has only ~240M active parameters; the authors argue it can run on-device. If you are evaluating multi-vector retrieval, measure storage on your own corpus first—that is the unanswered question in the report.

papers.title: OneLatent: Latent Reasoning for Efficient Foundation Recommendation Models
papers.authors: Hao Jiang, Peiru Du, Pengfei Yao, Mengting Li, Siyuan Lou, Kuo Cai, Sheng Yu, Qiang Luo, Jian Liang, Ruiming Tang, Fei P...
papers.summary: When an LLM serves as a recommendation foundation model, generating a natural-language reasoning trace (CoT) before outputting the item's semantic ID (SID) makes the output long and cuts throughput. Kuaishou's OneLatent inserts 3 learnable special tokens between the user context and the target SID: training first makes the model reproduce a teacher LLM's reasoning text after these 3 tokens, then switches to predicting the SID directly after them; at serving time only these 3 tokens are fed and no reasoning text is generated. The teacher writes reasoning from three angles: inferring intent, scoring the clicked item, and explaining why it was clicked. On the industrial dataset, SID@64 is 17.44% higher than OneReason-CoT's reason-then-answer mode; but against the strongest baseline trained on the same teacher reasoning and answering directly, the gain is only 1.58%, so most of the improvement comes from the teacher reasoning data. ==The reasoning slots are fixed at 3, so decoding does not grow with reasoning length==, and throughput is 17.49x that of explicit reasoning. A local-services advertising A/B test estimates a 9.6% revenue lift.

deep_reading.content_html:
When a large language model serves as a recommendation foundation model, one approach is to have the model first write a natural-language reasoning trace (CoT) and then output the semantic ID (SID, an identifier that maps an item to a three-level discrete code) of the next item. The reasoning text is far longer than a three-level SID, so it holds back both decoding time and throughput; moreover, earlier work on OneReason already reported that reasoning first and then answering does not consistently beat answering directly with the same model. Kuaishou's OneLatent appends 3 fixed special tokens after the user context and trains in several steps: first the model learns to reproduce a teacher LLM's reasoning text after these 3 tokens, then it is switched to outputting the target SID directly after them; at serving time only these 3 tokens are appended and no reasoning text is generated. On Kuaishou's local-services industrial data, OneLatent reaches SID@64 of 0.1993, 17.44% higher than OneReason-CoT in reason-then-answer mode, and its inference throughput is 17.49 times that of explicit reasoning, essentially the same as direct prediction without reasoning. Against the strongest baseline trained on the same teacher reasoning data and answering directly, the 3 latent tokens add only 1.58% on the industrial data, which shows that most of the gain comes from the teacher reasoning data itself. An online A/B test on 5% of traffic estimates a 9.6% revenue lift, and the model is now serving all traffic.

1. Why explicit reasoning works poorly in recommendation

The input of a foundation recommendation model (FRM) is the user profile Pu​, the chronologically ordered interaction history Hu​ and the request-time context Cu​ (time, location, search terms and so on); the output is the SID of the next item the user interacts with. Making the model write reasoning first causes two problems. One is cost: every request must decode the whole reasoning text token by token. The other is that accuracy does not necessarily rise: an extra generation path sits between the reasoning text and the SID, and if the reasoning goes off by one step, the SID that follows goes off with it. In the paper's Table 2, OneReason-CoT in reason-first mode reaches SID@64 of 0.1697 on the industrial data, below the 0.1823 of the same checkpoint answering directly.

The authors' idea is to use the teacher's reasoning only as a training signal and keep the reasoning process in the model's internal hidden states, with no text output at inference.

2. Method

2.1 What the latent tokens are

The authors add 3 special tokens ⟨L1​⟩⟨L2​⟩⟨L3​⟩ to the vocabulary, and all samples share this same set of token IDs. When the Transformer reaches these 3 positions it produces hidden states that vary with the context, and the SID tokens that follow read those hidden states through ordinary causal attention. There is no extra encoder, projection layer or decoder; the only added compute at inference is the fixed 3 tokens. The authors also state explicitly that later tokens can still see the raw context directly, so there is no guarantee that all the reasoning information is compressed into these 3 positions.

2.2 Teacher reasoning: three views, length adjusted to difficulty

The teacher model is Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507, which writes reasoning for each sample from three views:

  • Exploration: given only the user profile and history, the teacher infers the user's likely consumption intents and outputs reasoning plus a list of intents.
  • Evaluation: additionally told the item the user actually interacted with, the teacher judges how well that item matches the user's evidence and outputs reasoning plus a score from 1 to 5.
  • Attribution: told that this item is a positive sample, the teacher explains which historical signals led to the interaction.

The evaluation and attribution views use the true item, but this information goes only to the teacher and never enters the student model's input, so the answer does not leak. The prompt also asks the teacher to first judge how complex the evidence is: samples with a clear signal converge quickly, and samples with conflicting signals get a multi-dimensional comparison. The resulting reasoning drops to 65% of its original average length (taking the non-adaptive average length as 100), and on the longest tenth of samples the semantic similarity between the two kinds of reasoning is about 0.92.

2.3 Three-stage alignment and post-training

The student model is initialized from Qwen3.5-0.8B and first pretrained on the recommendation domain so that SIDs and item text descriptions can generate each other:
Lsem​=−logpϕ​(Sv​∣Cv​)−logpϕ​(Cv​∣Sv​)
Here Sv​ is the three-level SID of item v and Cv​ is its text description. The latent tokens are then trained in three stages:

  • Stage I: the input is "profile, history, view marker, 3 latent tokens", and the target is to reproduce one view's teacher reasoning.
  • Stage II: the same input, with the target changed to all of that sample's view reasonings. The loss of each reasoning is averaged over its tokens, so that long reasoning does not take a larger share of the loss.
  • Stage III: the request context is added to the input, and the target changes from reasoning text to the SID of the next item.

Post-training first runs curriculum fine-tuning from high-activity to low-activity users, then trains on a 1:1 mix of "append latent tokens, then predict the SID" and "predict the SID directly without latent tokens", so that both modes remain usable.

3. Experiments

3.1 Main results

This experiment compares OneLatent with three groups of baselines: item-ID-based sequential recommenders (GRU4Rec, BERT4Rec, HSTU), SID-based generative recommenders (TIGER, OneRec), and reasoning-enhanced models based on OneReason. There are two datasets: 7 days of industrial logs from Kuaishou local services (test set of 20,393 instances), and Kuaishou's public LLM-Rec benchmark (test set of 10,000). The metric Hit@64 indicates whether the correct item appears among the top 64 results the model generates. The table below is taken from the paper's Table 2; NoThink and Think are the direct-answer and reason-first modes of the same checkpoint, and the parentheses give the reasoning data used for training:

OneLatent is highest on every metric. But the source of the gain must be read from two separate comparisons. Against Think mode, industrial SID@64 is 17.44% higher; and when trained on the same three-view data, Think mode reaches only 0.1505 while OneLatent reaches 0.1993, which shows that for the same reasoning data, having the model write it out token by token before answering actually lowers accuracy, because the SID is generated only after the reasoning is finished and any error in the reasoning carries over to the SID. Against the strongest non-OneLatent result in each column, industrial SID@64 is only 1.58% higher and ID@64 only 0.45% higher; on the public data the gains are 12.21% and 19.10%. The strongest baseline on the industrial data is the model trained on evaluation-view reasoning that answers directly, and it already captures most of the gain.

On the 9B backbone, OneLatent reaches SID@64 of 0.2008, 8.13% above the best same-size non-latent result of 0.1857 (paper Table 3).

3.2 Inference efficiency

This experiment checks the inference overhead of the latent tokens. The authors compare three inference modes on 872 test instances (paper Table 7):

MethodTotal time (s)QPS
Direct prediction (no reasoning)3.17274.56
Explicit reasoning55.5915.68
OneLatent3.17274.29

OneLatent's throughput is 17.49 times that of explicit reasoning and nearly identical to direct prediction, because each request processes only 3 extra fixed tokens and does not need to decode reasoning text token by token. The paper's conclusion says "more than 10 times", which disagrees with the 17.49 times in the body; the number in the table is used here.

3.3 Quality and role of the teacher reasoning

This experiment checks whether the three-view reasoning is better than the original reasoning. The authors have GPT-5.5 score 100 samples of each kind of reasoning from 1 to 5 on nine dimensions (factuality, evidence use, causal logic and so on): OneReason's original reasoning averages 3.14, the adaptive-length reasoning 3.54, and the exploration, evaluation and attribution views 4.16, 4.33 and 4.03 (paper Table 4). Training OneLatent on different reasoning data raises public SID@64 from 0.0092 with the original reasoning to 0.0239 with the three views merged, and the evaluation view alone reaches 0.0233 (paper Table 5).

As the number of latent tokens goes from 1 to 3, the hit rates of all three SID levels rise; with 4 or 5 tokens they no longer improve consistently, so 3 are used in the end.

To see what is stored in the latent tokens, the authors feed the profile, view marker and 3 latent tokens to the trained model, deliberately leaving out the interaction history, have it generate reasoning text, and compare its semantic similarity with the teacher's reasoning; the cosine similarities of the three views are between 0.79 and 0.80 (paper Table 8). The authors themselves note that the profile is still visible, so this similarity only shows an association and cannot prove that the reasoning information is all stored in the latent tokens.

3.4 Deployment and A/B test

Even without reasoning text, calling the foundation model synchronously for every request still exceeds the latency and throughput budget. OneLatent is therefore deployed as a separate retrieval channel: new user behavior triggers asynchronous inference, refresh priority is set by user value and behavior strength, the generated candidates are written to Redis, and online requests take candidates from the cache, where they compete with the existing retrieval results in fine ranking. The A/B test ran in a sub-scenario of Kuaishou's local-services advertising, with 5% of traffic each for the treatment and control groups, from September 3 to 10, 2026. The treatment group's impressions rose 2.566%, ad spend rose 5.157%, and the posterior estimate of revenue rose 9.6%.

4. Limitations

The paper has no separate limitations section; in the body the authors acknowledge two points: the latent tokens are not a strict information bottleneck, and the reasoning information may be spread across the whole model; and the gain in Table 6 comes from the complete training pipeline and cannot be attributed to the latent tokens alone.

Two further points deserve attention. First, on the industrial data OneLatent is only 1.58% above the direct-answer model trained on the same teacher data, and the paper reports no variance across runs, so it is impossible to judge whether this gap is stable. Second, the online deployment uses an asynchronous cache, with candidates generated after the user's last behavior; the paper does not separate how much of the A/B gain comes from latent reasoning and how much from adding one more retrieval channel.

5. Practical implications

First, to give a recommendation model reasoning ability, the teacher's reasoning can first be used as training data rather than requiring the model to generate reasoning online. In the paper, the same three-view reasoning data reaches industrial SID@64 of 0.1993 when used as a training signal, but only 0.1505 when the model must write it out before answering.

Second, when evaluating "latent reasoning" methods, include a direct-answer model trained on the same teacher data as a baseline. On the industrial data in this paper, most of the gain already appears in that baseline, and comparing only against explicit reasoning overstates the effect of the latent tokens themselves.

papers.title: Chunk Recomputation under Real Document Revisions: Measuring Update Cost and Retrieval Quality of Fixed, Recursive, and Content-Defined Chunking
papers.authors: Yuning Bian, Lele Xu, Yifan Yuan, Xinyu Yin, Chengyan Zhan
papers.summary: RAG chunking schemes are usually compared on one static corpus, but knowledge bases keep changing. Each chunk is embedded on its own, so when an edit moves a chunk boundary, unchanged text must be re-embedded too. The authors measure this on 120 pairs of adjacent Chinese and English Wikipedia revisions, reusing an old vector only when a chunk's embedding input is byte-identical: non-overlapping fixed-size chunking recomputes 57–68% of the new version's embedding input, paragraph-first recursive chunking 38–56%, and content-defined chunking (CDC, which picks cut points from local text fingerprints) 43–54%, while evidence recall under a 2048-token retrieval budget differs by less than 2 percentage points among the three. When 1% of text is inserted at the start of an article, fixed-size chunking recomputes everything, ==because every window after the insertion point shifts, so no chunk matches the old version==. For knowledge bases that change often, ==a chunker's recompute fraction should be reported alongside its retrieval quality==.

deep_reading.content_html:
Chunking schemes for RAG are almost always compared on one static corpus, yet the documents in a knowledge base keep changing. Each chunk is embedded on its own, so if an edit moves a chunk boundary, the chunks on either side become new embedding inputs even when not a single word in them changed. This 6-page short paper measures that update cost directly: the authors take 120 pairs of adjacent revisions of Chinese and English Wikipedia articles, allow an old vector to be reused only when a chunk's complete embedding input is byte-identical to one in the old version, and compare three chunking methods with a frozen BGE-M3 encoder. On the 116 articles where all three methods succeed, non-overlapping fixed-size chunking recomputes 57–68% of the new version's embedding input, paragraph-first recursive chunking 38–56%, and content-defined chunking (CDC) 43–54%; under a 2048-token retrieval budget, the three differ in evidence recall by less than 2 percentage points within each language. Fixed-size chunking shifts everything after the insertion point, so none of the downstream windows can match the old version, which is why it recomputes the most. Which of recursive chunking and CDC is cheaper flips as the chunk-length parameters change.

1. Why measure update cost

An English article had only 0.13% of its text edited, yet fixed-size chunking recomputed 49% of its embedding input while paragraph-first chunking recomputed only 8%. This example from the paper's dataset shows that the amount edited and the amount recomputed can be far apart, and the gap is determined by the chunking rule.

For a knowledge base that is continually updated, the amount recomputed maps directly to embedding compute and to writes into the vector index. Earlier chunking evaluations only compared retrieval quality, but two schemes with similar retrieval quality can differ a lot in update cost: on the English articles in this paper, fixed-size chunking's mean recompute fraction is 1.5 times that of paragraph-first chunking (57% vs 38%). The authors want to answer three questions: how much each of the three chunking methods must recompute; whether that amount is driven by edit size, edit position or cut-point rules; and whether the scheme that recomputes less also retrieves worse.

2. Measurement

The reuse rule is strict: a chunk's complete embedding input (its text plus the encoder's special tokens) must be byte-identical to the input of some chunk in the old version for the old vector to be reused; a single differing character makes it a new input. The cache holds only the previous version of the same document and does not match across documents. The recompute fraction is defined as:
Rc​=∑x∈Uc​(Dnew​)​T(x)∑x∈Mc​​T(x)​
Here Uc​(Dnew​) is the set of distinct embedding inputs that chunking method c produces on the new version, Mc​ is the part of it not found in the old version's cache, and $T(x)$ is the number of input tokens of chunk x. Rc​=0 means everything is reused and Rc​=1 means everything is recomputed. The authors also run a no-edit control: chunking the same version twice must give Rc​=0, otherwise it counts as a pipeline failure.

All three chunking methods see only the current version and fixed parameters, never how the old version was chunked:

  • Fixed-size chunking: greedily cuts non-overlapping windows of at most 304 tokens.
  • Recursive chunking: splits any span longer than the 400-token target, preferring blank lines, then line breaks, then sentence-ending punctuation, and falls back to fixed windows only when none works; it then greedily packs the small units up to the target length.
  • CDC: uses the Steadlith implementation, which computes Rabin rolling fingerprints over the word sequence and places a cut wherever the fingerprint meets a condition, with chunk lengths limited to 176–352 tokens. The method was originally built for file-system deduplication; cut points depend only on nearby content, so inserting bytes near the front of a file does not move the cut points after it.

The chunk-length parameters of the three methods were tuned in advance so that their median chunk lengths are close (the actual maximum ratio is 1.17).

Retrieval quality is measured as follows: each article has two questions, 240 in total, and annotators mark on each version the character spans that answer the question. At retrieval time a batch of articles is put into one candidate pool, chunks are ranked by dot product, and whole chunks are packed into a 2048-token budget in rank order; recall is 1 if the packed chunks cover one complete evidence set.

3. Experiments

3.1 Main result: fixed-size chunking recomputes the most, recall differs little

This experiment answers how much each method must recompute and whether retrieval quality differs. The authors average the recompute fraction and evidence recall with fixed parameters over the 116 articles where all three methods succeed (paper Table I):

LanguageChunkingRecompute fractionEvidence recallMedian chunk length (tokens)
ChineseFixed-size68.4%97.4%304
ChineseRecursive55.7%98.3%356
ChineseCDC54.0%98.3%314
EnglishFixed-size57.4%96.7%304
EnglishRecursive37.9%96.8%342
EnglishCDC42.8%95.0%291

Paired by article, recursive chunking recomputes 12.7 percentage points less than fixed-size chunking (Chinese, 95% interval −19.7 to −6.2) and 19.6 points less (English); CDC recomputes 14.4 and 14.7 points less than fixed-size chunking. Paired differences in recall range from −1.9 to +0.9 points, with all intervals including or touching 0. The authors state explicitly that these intervals cannot rule out a drop in recall and do not prove equivalence, so they do not rank the methods by recall.

Recursive chunking's advantage is smaller in Chinese than in English because of its cut-point rules: Chinese sentence-ending punctuation is usually not followed by a space, so overly long Chinese paragraphs cannot be cut at sentence boundaries and fall back to fixed windows.

The smaller the edit, the larger the gap. On the 28 English articles with small edits (at most 5% edited), fixed-size chunking recomputes 46% on average, recursive chunking 25% and CDC 27%; on the 23 Chinese small-edit articles the figures are 62%, 45% and 36%. When more than 50% is edited, all three must recompute 60–90%.

3.2 Edit position: why fixed-size chunking recomputes so much

This experiment tests whether "boundary shift" is the main source of recomputation. It changes only one variable: the same 1% insertion is placed at the start, middle or end of the article, with everything else unchanged. Result: fixed-size chunking falls from 100% for an insertion at the start to about 12% for one at the end, because every window after the insertion point moves back by the length of the insertion and no downstream chunk can be reused. Recursive chunking and CDC stay below 30% at all three positions, as paragraph breaks and content-fingerprint cut points realign quickly after the edit.

The authors also run a verbatim check: how much of the recomputed input is text that already exists unchanged in the old version. On English articles, 50% of the tokens fixed-size chunking recomputes are text present verbatim in the old version, 33% for CDC and 12% for recursive chunking (47%, 45% and 37% in Chinese). This text was not changed at all; it was only cut into different chunks, so recomputing it is caused entirely by the cut-point rule.

3.3 Whether recursive chunking or CDC is cheaper depends on parameters

This experiment checks whether the ranking of the two content-aware methods is stable. Without retuning, the authors try 6 target chunk lengths between 256 and 496 tokens for each method and compare paired settings whose median-length ratio is at most 1.15. Result: the CDC-minus-recursive recompute difference ranges from −2.4 to +6.2 points in English and from −0.7 to +5.5 in Chinese, flipping sign in both languages. For example, in English raising recursive chunking's target length from 400 to 448 raises its recompute fraction from 37.9% to 46.2%, while CDC at the same 448 is 43.8%. The reason is that recursive chunking packs several small paragraphs into one chunk; once an edit changes one paragraph's length, the packing of several following paragraphs can change too, and the larger the target length, the farther this chain reaction propagates. Fixed-size chunking recomputes the most in every setting.

The authors checked the cost once more on the arXivEdits paper-revision data: the mean recompute fractions of fixed-size, recursive and CDC chunking are 94.5%, 81.4% and 80.2%, with fixed-size still highest. The text-extraction noise of this dataset is unquantified, so it serves only as side evidence on cost.

3.4 Overlapping windows are not the fix

A common remedy is to let adjacent fixed windows overlap by 32 or 64 tokens. The result is a recompute fraction within 1.3 points of the non-overlapping version, 10–26% more total embedding input, and English recall down by 3.0 and 3.9 points, because the duplicated text uses up the 2048-token retrieval budget.

4. Limitations

The authors list these limitations: Wikipedia is the only source; the annotations of the 240 questions were not independently adjudicated by multiple people, and when the authors spot-checked 60 labels themselves, 57 agreed; the median chunk-length ratio of the three methods is 1.17, above the preset 1.15; only one encoder is used; and the related method KARA was not run. CDC failed on 4 Chinese articles because CDC splits words on spaces, so a long run of Chinese text without spaces is treated as a single unit of 403–550 tokens, exceeding the 352 maximum.

Two further points deserve attention. First, all three methods recovered all the evidence in 105 of the 116 articles, and recall is generally above 95%, close to the ceiling, so this retrieval setup cannot distinguish small quality differences between methods. Second, the recompute fraction measures embedding input and is not converted into latency or cost; if embedding is a small part of the whole update pipeline, for example when index rebuilding or review costs more, a gap of a few tens of percentage points is diluted in the total cost.

5. Practical implications

First, if a knowledge base is edited often and in small amounts, do not use non-overlapping fixed-size chunking. Switching to paragraph-first recursive chunking takes the mean recompute fraction on English articles from 57% to 38%, and from 46% to 25% on small-edit articles, with retrieval recall essentially unchanged. The precondition is to use the byte-identical input as the cache key, so that vectors are reused whenever the text has not changed.

Second, when evaluating chunking schemes, report the recompute fraction together with retrieval quality, and measure both under your own chunk-length parameters. The ranking of recursive chunking and CDC flips with parameters, so no ranking in the paper can be carried over as is. For Chinese corpora, check whether the cut-point rules rely on spaces; otherwise recursive chunking falls back to fixed windows and CDC fails outright.

papers.title: Directional Posterior Feedback Fusion for Query Reformulation in Dense Retrieval
papers.authors: Yiteng Tu, Qingyi Pan, Weihang Su, Jiaxin Mao, Yiqun Liu, Qingyao Ai
papers.summary: When rewriting a query vector with first-round retrieved documents or an LLM-written hypothetical answer (HyDE), the usual approach averages feedback vectors and interpolates with the original query. DIFF argues that ==each piece of feedback only supports correcting the query along one direction, so other directions should not be pulled back by it==: it subtracts the component parallel to the original query to get each feedback's rotation direction and magnitude, constrains only the projection of the correction onto that direction, weights by query–feedback similarity and group agreement, and solves a K×K linear system—without training any model. On 14 BEIR subsets, bge-base with HyDE rises from 0.5492 to 0.5717 mean NDCG@10; with retrieved-document feedback, vector averaging falls to 0.5045 while DIFF scores 0.5522.

deep_reading.content_html:
In vector retrieval, short queries often under-specify intent. A common fix is to gather feedback text—top documents from a first-round search, or an LLM-written hypothetical answer (HyDE)—and use it to update the query vector. Most methods average the feedback vectors or linearly interpolate with the original query, treating each feedback as "what the new query should look like" and pulling the query toward it as a whole. Tsinghua's DIFF argues that this causes interference: each piece of feedback usually supports correcting the query along only one direction; other directions carry no information from it, yet are still pulled back. DIFF first extracts the direction each feedback adds beyond the original query, requires the corrected query to agree with the feedback only along that direction, weights constraints by feedback quality, adds a "do not drift too far from the original" term, and has a closed-form solution that needs no training. On 14 BEIR subsets, 3 retrievers, and 4 feedback sources, DIFF's mean NDCG@10 is best or tied for best in 12 of 12 settings, but with first-round retrieved documents as feedback it barely improves over the unfeedbacked query.

1. Treating feedback as target points loses complementary information

Let the original query be q and the correction proposed by feedback i relative to q be ei​=ℓi​ui​, with unit direction ui​ and magnitude ℓi​. Pointwise fitting minimizes ∥δ−ℓi​ui​∥2. The authors split it:
∥δ−ℓi​ui​∥2=(ui⊤​δ−ℓi​)2+∥(I−ui​ui⊤​)δ∥2
The first term asks δ's component along ui​ to equal ℓi​—desired. The second penalizes δ on every other direction, which may be exactly what other feedback supports. Example: query "apple event"; one feedback doc is about a new phone, another about a new laptop; pointwise fitting pulls the query halfway between them and travels only halfway on each direction.

They prove that under the same weights, directional constraints yield a correction magnitude at least as large as pointwise fitting, with equality only when all feedback directions are collinear; when feedback directions are pairwise orthogonal, pointwise fitting dilutes each direction's correction by the other feedbacks' weights.

2. Method: four steps

Step 1: new direction per feedback. All vectors are L2-normalized on the unit sphere. For feedback fi​, compute similarity si​=q⊤fi​, then subtract the component parallel to q to get ri​=fi​−si​q. Direction ui​ is where this feedback wants to rotate the query; length ℓi​ equals the sine of their angle—how much new content it adds.

Step 2: credibility per feedback. Credibility τi​=g⋅ai​ has two layers. Per-item quality ai​: standardize the si​ values under the same query by median and MAD, then pass through a sigmoid, so feedback closer to the query weighs more without depending on absolute similarity scales across models. Group credibility g: mean of all correction vectors μ, then compare ∥μ∥2 to dispersion around that mean; g is high when directions agree and low when they conflict, then multiplied by mean per-item quality.

Step 3: jointly solve for the correction. The objective keeps only each feedback's own-direction constraint plus a penalty on correction size:
δ∗=argδmin​ 2λ​∥δ∥2+21​i∑​τi​(ui⊤​δ−ℓi​)2
It has a closed form: solve a K×K linear system (K feedbacks, 5 in the main experiment), cost O(K2D+K3) for dimension D.

Step 4: map back to the sphere. The final rotation angle is the min of ∥δ∗∥ and "g × max allowed angle", then q′=cosϕq+sinϕδ∗/∥δ∗∥. When the group is untrustworthy, g is small and the query barely moves.

3. Experiments

Setup: 14 BEIR subsets (ArguAna, FEVER, HotpotQA, MSMARCO, NQ, SciFact, TREC-COVID, …), three retrievers bge-base-en-v1.5, e5-base-v2, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. Feedback is either the top-K first-round documents (PRF) or three Qwen3.8-27B generations (HyDE hypothetical docs, Q2D query expansion, CoT reasoning). All methods share the same encoder, the same feedback, and the same index—only fusion differs. Baselines include vector averaging (VPRF), concatenate-and-reencode (Concat-P/L), orthogonal-component OR-PRF, dimension-weighted DIME and Eclipse, and AnchorQE which needs extra retrieval to estimate weights.

3.1 Main results

This checks whether DIFF beats other fusion methods across retrievers and feedback sources. Mean NDCG@10 over 14 subsets; parentheses are the unfeedbacked query:

Two results stand out. First, with retrieved-document feedback, simple averaging (VPRF) pulls scores below the original query—on BGE from 0.5492 to 0.5045; DIFF in that column merely does not lose: 0.5522 on BGE, 0.5252 on E5, 0.5491 on Qwen, barely changing versus the original. Second, with LLM-generated feedback every method gains; DIFF reaches 0.5717 on BGE with HyDE and 0.5777 on Qwen. It is close to AnchorQE (0.5717 vs 0.5700 on BGE + HyDE) but needs no extra retrieval for weights.

3.2 Ablations

This checks whether directional constraints and credibility weighting are each necessary. On BGE, remove or replace one part at a time:

Switching back to pointwise fitting is among the largest drops, directly supporting the paper's core claim: constraining each feedback only along its own direction beats pulling the query toward feedback as a whole. Dropping per-item quality under HyDE falls from 0.5717 to 0.5481—generated hypothetical docs vary in quality and must be treated differently.

3.3 Feedback count

As K grows from 1 to 20, VPRF drops quickly under retrieved-document feedback because later documents are noisier. DIFF stays stable across K; the authors attribute this to group credibility shrinking the correction when feedback becomes mixed.

4. Limitations

The main-table point: with first-round retrieved documents as feedback, DIFF barely beats the unfeedbacked query and is slightly worse on Qwen (0.5491 vs 0.5492). Its value is mainly "not being dragged down by noise" and "using generated feedback well." Experiments are only on BEIR with retrievers up to 0.6B; production-scale corpora and larger embedding models are untested. Group credibility and max rotation angle have hyperparameters whose sensitivity is not analyzed in the body.

5. Takeaways

If you already use HyDE or query expansion and average the encoded text with the original query, consider DIFF: it depends only on vectors, needs no training and no extra retrieval, and solves one 5×5 linear system per query. If feedback is first-round retrieval, this paper's results say gains are limited—at least confirm that averaging is not already hurting metrics.

papers.title: FLINT: Fixed-budget Late Interaction
papers.authors: Himank Handa, Negar Arabzadeh, Matei Zaharia
papers.summary: FLINT pools both queries and documents into a fixed number of vectors. This preserves late interaction while bounding storage and matching work. On long-query corpora, end-to-end retrieval is 1.5–2.8 times faster than ConstBERT.
papers.key_insight: Budget vectors on both sides of retrieval. Compressing documents alone reduces storage, but long queries still drive many comparisons; symmetric pooling bounds both costs.

papers.title: UIBK-Embedding: Effective Text Retrieval by Unifying Dense and Late-Interaction Retrieval
papers.authors: Abdelrahman Abdallah, Mohammed Ali, Adam Jatowt
papers.summary: One encoder combines global semantics with token matching. Tagged extra vectors make standard MaxSim equal token-level matching plus a weighted dense score, so existing late-interaction indexes remain usable. BEIR nDCG@10 reaches 59.79.
papers.key_insight: A hybrid representation can remove the need for separate encoders, indexes and score fusion. Distilling the final combined score also aligns training with the score actually served.

papers.title: Optimal Fusion Weights Form Intervals, Not Points: A Latency-Aware Study of Query-Adaptive WRRF
papers.authors: Iris Ma, Zahra Shekarchi, Stuart Mcilroy, Mahtab Farrokh, Fattane Zarrinkalam, Joel Stremmel
papers.summary: Adaptive fusion need not predict one exact weight. Across 128 configurations, 74 significantly outperform standard RRF after multiple-testing correction.
papers.key_insight: Treat optimal weights as sets rather than arbitrary point targets, and include predictor latency in deployment decisions.

papers.title: EKLAV: Elicited Key CoT Learning via Answer only superVision
papers.authors: Adarsh Singh, Aman Singh, Kushal Raj Bhandari, Soham Dan, Anoop Kumar, Vivek Gupta
papers.summary: EKLAV provides teacher reasoning as training context while supervising only answers. It wins 41 of 48 model-domain comparisons on BRIGHT reranking.
papers.key_insight: Reasoning traces need not be imitation targets. Changing where supervision applies can reuse a fixed teacher corpus with less training and inference work.

papers.title: Preference Is Not Position: Evaluating Reranking on NevIR in Fixed Hybrid Candidate Pools
papers.authors: Yuning Bian, Lele Xu, Yifan Yuan, Xinyu Yin, Chengyan Zhan
papers.summary: Correct pairwise preference does not guarantee a useful list position. Bounded Qwen3 reranking reaches preferred-passage MRR of 0.7509 in fixed hybrid pools.
papers.key_insight: Evaluate pair preference and full-list position separately; optimizing one can degrade the other.

papers.title: OpenSaC: A Python Library for Search as Code in Deep Research Agents
papers.authors: Qi Liu, Jiaxin Mao, Fengbin Zhu, Tat-Seng Chua, Ji-Rong Wen
papers.summary: OpenSaC lets research agents write programs that combine search, reading, reranking, and local processing, returning selected evidence to the model. On BrowseComp, it cuts model-token use by 37.8%.
papers.key_insight: Process intermediate evidence in code and preserve source links for reuse. The library reduces repeated model reading, but requires an execution environment. WideSearch row F1 falls slightly, so efficiency gains do not guarantee better answers.

papers.title: FALCA: Falsification-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Deep Search Agents
papers.authors: Zijun Dou, Kun Luo, Chaofan Li, Shuqi Lu, Zheng Liu
papers.summary: Deep search can reinforce an early mistaken hypothesis. FALCA separates answer proposals from independent counterevidence searches and trains research-state revision with hierarchical credit. Its 4B model reaches 56.0% accuracy on BrowseComp.
papers.key_insight: Give counterevidence checking its own context. A useful falsification report names conflicting evidence and unmet constraints, giving the next search a specific gap to resolve.

papers.title: ClueFlow: Learning Long-Horizon Search through Attributed Research-State Transitions
papers.authors: Yicheng Wang, Wentao Tan, Yidan Huang, Yifei Liu, Qiong Cao
papers.summary: ClueFlow links browser actions to research-state updates and the final answer. It uses those attribution chains for supervised learning and turn-level RL. In a controlled comparison, selected supervision matches all-turn SFT with about 30% of its training tokens.
papers.key_insight: Record how evidence changes the research state. Verified local progress can remain useful even when the final answer is wrong, recovering training signals that whole-trajectory rejection would discard.

papers.title: EG-GRPO: Evidence-Guided Step-level Credit Assignment for Deep Search Agents
papers.authors: Sijia Luo, Mengjie Gao, Yuxiao He, Mengshu Sun, Cuiping Li, Hong Chen, Jing Zhang
papers.summary: EG-GRPO rewards the first search step that finds support for a required claim, then compares actions from similar evidence states. The 4B agent reaches 45.9% accuracy on GAIA.
papers.key_insight: Reward newly acquired evidence rather than repeated citations. Conditioning comparisons on what an agent already knows reduces unfair comparisons between early and nearly finished trajectories; fallback grouping handles sparse state matches.

papers.title: Grounded Credit Assignment in Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Search Agents
papers.authors: Qirui Liu, Hao Chen, Yi Wen, Weijie Shi, Yao Zhao, Xianhe Chen, Hao Zhao, Xing Tang, Weihong Luo, Yuyu Luo
papers.summary: A search agent can answer correctly without using retrieved evidence. Grounded Credit Assignment separates credit for finding evidence from credit for answering. On the larger evaluated model, it improves average exact match over Search-R1 by 6.3 percentage points.
papers.key_insight: Reward evidence acquisition separately from answer correctness. Otherwise, a lucky answer from memory credits the entire retrieval trace and can improve accuracy while weakening grounding. The proposed correction uses verifiable sub-outcomes without an extra reward model.

papers.title: Let Agents Design How They Search: Automatic Interface Optimization for Agentic Search
papers.authors: Sangjune An, Jaeyoon Jung, Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek, Junmo Cho, Sung Ju Hwang, Hae Beom Lee
papers.summary: Korea University and KAIST have Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) design retrieval tools for a search agent: it reads each question's execution log and score, jointly edits pre-generated index files, executable search scripts, and usage instructions, and after 10 rounds keeps the best version on the optimization set. With GPT-5.4-nano as the search agent, BrowseComp-Plus accuracy rises from DCI's 71.6% to 78.4%, and mean nDCG@10 on four BRIGHT subsets from 45.7 to 55.0. Prompt-only optimization reaches 75.6% and 52.0, ==so the rest of the gain comes from the generated index files and search scripts==; handing the interface unchanged to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite still beats DCI (73.9% vs 60.9%).

deep_reading.content_html:
When an LLM agent searches a document corpus, the tools it may use, how the corpus is pre-organized, and how the prompt teaches it to use those tools together form the "search interface." Today's interfaces are hand-designed and shared across corpora—for example DCI gives the agent a shell and lets it grep/cat raw documents. Korea University and KAIST's SearchWeaver has another coding agent (Claude Code + Claude Opus 5.5) design that interface automatically: it reads the search agent's full execution log and per-question scores, finds failure causes, then edits three things at once—pre-generated index files, executable search scripts, and the search agent's usage instructions—reruns, scores, and loops for 10 rounds. With GPT-5.4-nano as the search agent, BrowseComp-Plus accuracy rises from DCI's 71.6% to 78.4%, and mean nDCG@10 on four BRIGHT subsets from 45.7 to 55.0; the optimized interface handed unchanged to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite also beats DCI.

1. One interface does not fit every corpus

Recent agentic retrieval methods all work on a fixed interface: RAG returns retriever passages; DCI lets the agent shell through raw docs; DR-DCI first vector-retrieves docs into a workspace then browses; RISE bounds a restricted workspace and adds model-generated tables of contents. Paper Table 1 shows relative ranking flips by corpus: DR-DCI beats DCI on BrowseComp-Plus (73.1% vs 71.6%) but loses on BRIGHT (42.1 vs 45.7). The authors conclude the interface should be designed for the specific corpus and model.

2. Method: let a coding agent iteratively edit the interface

2.1 What an interface contains

A candidate interface has three parts:

  • Pre-generated files: one-time processing of the whole corpus before any question arrives—for example a title→path index reused by every question.
  • Executable tools: Python scripts that may call provided BM25 and vector retrieval, restrict search to a subdirectory, or merge the agent's document judgments with retrieval ranks.
  • Usage instructions: instructions for the search agent on when to use which tool and how to verify clues.

Candidates may also replace the search agent's base system prompt and context-management policy. The search agent's model weights stay fixed.

2.2 Optimization loop

The designer is Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5). Each round it inspects the corpus and all prior candidates, writes a new interface; the new interface runs on the optimization questions and returns per-question scores plus full execution logs (commands, tool returns, final answer). Gold document IDs for optimization questions are also given to the designer to separate "not found" from "found but not recognized." Every candidate's outcome is kept for later reference regardless of quality. After 10 rounds, the interface with the best mean optimization-set score is evaluated on held-out test questions that never enter the designer's feedback.

3. Experiments

Setup. BrowseComp-Plus (BCP) answers multi-clue questions over a fixed web corpus, judged by GPT-4.1: 30 optimization / 800 test questions. BRIGHT is reasoning-heavy document retrieval on biology, earth science, economics, and robotics: 213 optimization / 210 test questions, scored by nDCG@10. Each corpus gets its own optimized interface. Retrieval resources for the designer: BM25 + Qwen3-Embedding-4B on BCP; BM25 + ReasonEmbed-Qwen3-8B rankings on BRIGHT.

3.1 Main results

This checks whether corpus-optimized interfaces beat fixed interfaces on both benchmarks and every subset:

Optimized strategies differ by corpus: biology restricts retrieval to a topic directory; earth science calls retrieval only when building the final ranking; economics and robotics fold the agent's document judgments into ranking—via document order for the former and relevance grades for the latter.

3.2 Tool time

Per-question tool time (excluding model inference) also falls versus DCI: BCP from 42.4 s to 32.9 s, BRIGHT from 63.2 s to 36.6 s. From the figure, RISE and DR-DCI use even less tool time; SearchWeaver spends more tool time for higher scores, and the authors place it on the Pareto front among evaluated methods.

3.3 Is prompt-only enough?

This checks whether gains come from generated files and tools, not only better prompts. Two variants: the same loop but only prompts may change (Prompt Optimization); and SearchWeaver's final interface with generated files, tools, and matching instructions removed, without re-optimizing.

Prompt-only also gains clearly and even beats SearchWeaver on the economics subset (41.8 vs 38.3). Overall, adding files and tools is better; removing them falls back near DCI.

3.4 Does it transfer across models?

This checks whether the interface reuses across models. The GPT-5.4-nano-optimized interface is handed unchanged to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite: BCP accuracy 73.9% (DCI 60.9%), BRIGHT mean nDCG@10 58.8 (DCI 50.7), and BRIGHT per-question tool time from 23.1 s to 15.5 s. It works without re-optimization, so a substantial part of what was optimized belongs to the corpus itself, not only to model-specific tricks.

4. Limitations

Experiments use a static corpus. Whether pre-generated indexes and dependent tools must be refreshed after document adds/deletes, and whether updates can be incremental, is explicitly unstudied. BCP optimizes on only 30 questions; overfitting to those 30 is not analyzed. Each optimization round has the designer (Claude Opus 5.5) read full execution logs and the search agent rerun the optimization set—that cost is unreported.

5. Takeaways

For teams building internal knowledge-base QA agents, this gives an operable loop: take a small set of questions with gold answers and let a coding agent generate index files and retrieval scripts from execution logs, rather than only tuning prompts. The ablation where prompt-only raises BCP from 71.6% to 75.6% is also useful—when resources are limited, start with cheap prompt optimization. If the corpus changes often, design your own index maintenance.

papers.title: MAPS: Macro-Adaptive Parallel Reasoning for Regulating Search Momentum in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Xinze Li, Dingwen Zhang, Zhenghao Liu, Yukun Yan, Shuo Wang, Yu Gu, Ge Yu, Maosong Sun
papers.summary: Northeastern University and Tsinghua find that in retrieve-while-reasoning RAG, ==later sub-queries keep drifting away from the original question along the direction earlier sub-queries already moved==, and the effect grows with step count. MAPS therefore makes two changes: each round only passes distilled knowledge and a compressed reasoning summary to the model, never historical sub-queries; before writing sub-queries it lists several complementary directions, writes one sub-query per direction, retrieves in parallel, and merges. On Qwen3-32B, mean Cover-EM over six QA sets is 56.0 versus 49.2 for ParallelSearch and 43.9 for Search-o1; removing any of the three components hurts.

deep_reading.content_html:
Retrieve-while-reasoning RAG methods such as Search-o1 have the LLM write the next sub-query from the full prior reasoning and sub-query history. Northeastern University and Tsinghua first measure the phenomenon: encode each sub-query as a vector, exponentially accumulate "adjacent sub-query vector differences" as "search momentum," and test whether that momentum predicts the direction of the next sub-query's drift from the original question. Prediction gets better at later steps, showing that later sub-queries tend to keep drifting along the direction earlier ones already took. MAPS therefore makes two changes: each round only passes retrieved knowledge and a compressed reasoning state to the model—never historical sub-queries or the full reasoning trace; each round first lists several complementary retrieval directions, writes one sub-query per direction, retrieves in parallel, and merges. On Qwen3-32B, MAPS mean Cover-EM (whether the gold answer appears in the response) over six QA sets is 56.0 versus 49.2 for ParallelSearch and 43.9 for Search-o1.

1. Sub-queries drift farther along existing directions

Multi-hop questions need evidence spread across documents, so models reason and emit sub-queries interleaved. The problem is that the sub-query at step t is conditioned on the entire prior trajectory; an early drift affects every later step.

The paper quantifies this with search momentum:

  1. Encode each sub-query as vector qt​ with E5.
  2. Momentum mt​=βt​⋅mt−1​+(1−βt​)⋅(qt​−qt−1​)—accumulate each step's movement with weight βt​; larger βt​ weights history more.
  3. Alignment St​=cos(mt​,qt+1​−q0​)—cosine between current momentum and the next sub-query's offset from the original question.
  4. Fit each step's βt​ on the training set with L-BFGS-B to maximize St​, and report St​ on a held-out set.

Both βt​ and St​ rise with step count: later steps weight historical movement more, and the next sub-query's offset aligns more with existing momentum. The authors' reading: the reasoning process does not self-correct early drift.

2. Method: MAPS

2.1 Do not show the model historical sub-queries

The usual approach feeds the full trajectory (reasoning, sub-queries, retrievals) every step. MAPS keeps only two things:

  • Knowledge observations: knowledge o1​…ot−1​ distilled from prior retrievals;
  • Compressed reasoning state: a per-round updated reasoning summary that excludes historical sub-queries.

Next-round reasoning is conditioned only on the original question, knowledge observations, and the compressed state. When knowledge is enough or the max round is hit, the same three inputs produce the final answer.

2.2 Parallel directions each round

Each round has three steps by three roles:

  1. Propose directions: from the original question, existing knowledge, and reasoning state, list N complementary retrieval directions;
  2. Write sub-queries: one sub-query per direction, retrieve top-K each, merge into one document set;
  3. Consolidate: merge evidence into this round's knowledge observation ot​ and update the compressed reasoning state.

3. Experiments

Setup. Single-hop: NQ, PopQA; multi-hop: 2WikiQA, HotpotQA, MuSiQue; reasoning: GPQA Diamond (198 questions); 1,000 random questions per set except GPQA. Backbones: Qwen3-32B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Corpus: December 2018 English Wikipedia; retriever E5-base-v2 + FAISS, top-5 passages, at most 10 rounds. Metric: Cover-EM.

3.1 Main results

This checks whether MAPS beats existing RAG methods across question types and both backbones.

ParallelSearch also emits multiple sub-queries in parallel; MAPS beats it on every dataset. The authors conclude that writing more sub-queries alone is not enough—the dependence on the historical trajectory must also be cut.

3.2 Ablations

This checks each of the three components: drop "list directions first" (write parallel sub-queries directly), drop parallelism (one direction per round), drop decoupling (keep the full historical trajectory).

Removing any component lowers the mean; GPQA drops the most. Note the ablation table's MAPS GPQA 62.3 / mean 56.1 disagrees with the main table's 62.1 / 56.0; the paper does not explain. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, dropping decoupling only slightly trails full MAPS on 2WikiQA (64.4) and GPQA (78.1).

3.3 Is momentum actually suppressed?

This checks whether MAPS gains come from less drift. Sample 500 questions across all sets; accumulate per-round change in cosine between momentum and the original question. As rounds grow, MAPS's cumulative offset is smaller and more stable than Search-o1 and the no-decoupling variant. Another analysis measures sub-query–gold-evidence similarity: Search-o1 falls throughout; MAPS falls early then recovers and stabilizes.

3.4 Stopping rounds

MAPS stops after round 1 on 62.7% of samples, above Search-o1's 50.4% and ParallelSearch's 58.5%; the share needing 5+ rounds is also higher (14.9% vs 12.5% and 5.1%). The authors' reading: easy questions gather enough evidence earlier, while hard ones do not stop too soon.

4. Limitations

No per-question model-call counts, token cost, or latency. Each MAPS round calls direction, sub-query, and consolidate roles plus N retrievals, so cost is likely above Search-o1, but how much is unknown. How N is chosen and how sensitive results are is also unreported. Experiments use 2018 Wikipedia and a relatively weak E5-base-v2 retriever; whether gaps hold with stronger retrievers is untested.

5. Takeaways

Multi-hop RAG agent teams can try two low-cost changes: each round, do not feed historical sub-queries back—only distilled knowledge and a reasoning summary; before writing sub-queries, have the model list complementary directions. Ablations show removing either hurts. Measure the added call cost yourself before shipping.

papers.title: Signals and Queries: Token-Efficient Agentic Context Discovery
papers.authors: Yam Marcovitz
papers.summary: Parlant used to ask an LLM whether each customer-service rule is relevant every turn—about 69,000 tokens for 36 rules. S&Q instead has an LLM offline write 10 triggering user messages and 10 easily confused counterexamples per rule and trains a logistic regressor; online each turn needs one embedding and 37 µs of CPU. On τ²-bench airline support at 90% recall, precision is 32%–34% versus 31% for a cosine threshold; after mining examples from real dialogues precision rises to 43.5%, and ==almost all of that lift comes from the counterexamples==.

deep_reading.content_html:
Customer-facing LLM agents are usually constrained by dozens of behavioral rules (policies)—for example "compensation only if the customer bought travel insurance." Every turn must decide which rules are relevant and put them in the prompt. Parlant's original approach asked an LLM "is this relevant now?" for every rule every turn—36 rules meant 36 calls and about 69,000 prompt tokens. Parlant's Signals and Queries (S&Q) replaces that with a small offline-trained classifier: for each rule an LLM offline writes 10 user messages that should trigger it and 10 that "look similar but should be handled by a neighboring rule", embeds them, and trains one logistic regression per rule; online each turn needs one embedding call and 36 vector dot products—37 µs of CPU. On 254 dialogue prefixes and 36 rules from τ²-bench airline support, with LLM judgments as gold, at ≥90% recall S&Q precision is 32% on Gemini embeddings and 34% on OpenAI embeddings versus 31% for a cosine threshold; after mining examples from real dialogues, precision rises to 43.5% (Gemini) and 41.6% (OpenAI).

1. Missing a rule is an error; adding an extra is only waste

Stuffing every rule into the prompt every turn hits middle-context neglect, diluted per-instruction attention, and harder full compliance as instruction count grows, while token cost grows linearly with rule count. So relevant rules must be filtered first.

The cost is asymmetric: missing a cancellation policy may let the agent approve an action that should be refused; adding an irrelevant rule only costs a few hundred tokens. S&Q therefore targets ≥90% recall per rule first, then precision. It is a pre-filter—dropped rules never come back; kept rules are still re-read by the agent model.

Direct vector similarity between dialogue and rule text is almost free, but dialogue is colloquial user speech and rules are formal text, so vectors separate poorly.

2. Method

2.1 Offline: positives and hard negatives per rule

For each rule, gemini-3.5-flash generates from the rule text alone:

  • signals (10): user messages that should trigger the rule—e.g. cancellation → "I want to cancel my flight to Chicago next week";
  • anti-signals (10): nearby-topic messages that another rule should handle—e.g. "I want to move my flight from Tuesday to Thursday" (a change rule).

No real dialogues are used in generation.

2.2 One logistic regression per rule

For each rule, train a logistic regression on the 20 message embeddings to output a "relevant" probability. Each rule's classifier depends only on its own examples, so adding or editing a rule only regenerates its examples and trains one classifier (~2 ms); other rules are untouched.

2.3 Online: max of two dialogue views

At turn t, score two vectors and take the max: the embedding of the dialogue so far, and the embedding of each user message so far. All vectors are centered by subtracting the mean of all rules then renormalized. A rule is kept if its score exceeds a global threshold θ. Taking the max over single user messages keeps earlier topics from diluting a later topic shift. Real-dialogue scores sit below generated examples, so θ is negative (Gemini −0.45, OpenAI −0.4).

3. Experiments

Setup. 50 airline-support dialogues from a Parlant agent and the τ²-bench user simulator; every user-message-ending prefix is a query state (254 total). 36 rules: 6 sections of the τ²-bench airline policy plus 30 author-written rules (identity checks, baggage claims, unaccompanied minors, fare rules, fraud, …), with intentional near-synonym groups. Gold labels: gemini-3.1-flash-lite scores each (prefix, rule) 1–5 with Parlant's online relevance prompt; ≥4 is relevant—9,144 labels. Metrics are macro-averaged over the 31 rules that appear at least once. Four baselines: cosine top-K or cosine-threshold against rule text or against signals. Embeddings: gemini-embedding-001 and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large, each run separately.

3.1 Recall–precision curves

This checks whether S&Q is more precise than vector retrieval at matched recall. The paper reports S&Q highest at every recall level, leading by ~4 points in the mid range (60–70% recall), with a smaller gap at high recall: +2.9 on OpenAI, only +0.9 on Gemini. Top-K even at K=15 (15 of 36) reaches only ~66% recall because the number of simultaneously relevant rules varies a lot per turn.

Best precision at ≥90% recall:

At that operating point S&Q beats a cosine threshold by only 1–3 points. Using signals alone (no classifier) is no better than rule text; the lift comes from a classifier with negatives.

3.2 Ablations

This checks which component matters, via AUPRC and precision at 90% recall.

Dropping negatives hurts most. Two findings go against the default: using other rules' signals as negatives is slightly better than dedicated anti-signals—the authors keep the latter so rules stay independent; whole-dialogue-only view also has higher AUPRC because benchmark dialogues are short and single-topic (median ~1,600 characters), so per-message max does not help here. They therefore add a synthetic test: concatenate two different-task dialogues as "A then B"; at 30% false-positive rate, per-message max raises recall on B-topic rules by 12–19 points versus the whole-dialogue view.

3.3 Does fine-tuning the encoder help?

Same local small model all-MiniLM-L6-v2: frozen encoder + logistic regression is 91% recall / 32% precision; SetFit fine-tuning the encoder is 90% / 31%. Fine-tuning does not help, and each rule would need an ~90 MB model versus ~12 KB for logistic weights.

3.4 Examples mined from real dialogues

This checks whether example quality is the bottleneck. Split dialogue scenes in half; mine from one half: the user message where a rule first reaches its max score as a signal; the most signal-like user message the model marks clearly irrelevant as an anti-signal; evaluate on the other half.

Swapping only positives barely moves (Gemini +0.5, OpenAI −1.5); almost all of the lift comes from mined negatives. The eval half has only 131 prefixes; the authors say this only indicates direction and rough magnitude.

4. Limitations

Gold labels are another LLM's judgments, not human labels. Even at 90% recall S&Q precision is only low thirties, so most kept rules are still irrelevant and need a later model filter. Mining examples needs relevance labels on real dialogues; in the half-split only 22 of 29 appearing rules got enough examples. In long dialogues a once-triggered rule stays forever—the keep set only grows; the authors note deployments need a separate expiry mechanism.

5. Takeaways

For customer agents with many rules or tool descriptions, replace "ask an LLM every turn whether this rule is relevant" with one offline linear classifier per rule; online cost falls to one embedding call. The highest-leverage investment is negatives: prepare easily confused counterexamples for neighboring rules, ideally mined from real dialogues.

papers.title: DeclineCraft: A RAG Abstention Benchmark for Jointly Measuring Combined Retrieval and Parametric Knowledge
papers.authors: Atharva Thakur, Abulhair Saparov, Bruno Ribeiro
papers.summary: DeclineCraft tests whether models abstain when neither retrieved evidence nor internal knowledge supports an answer. Version-specific Minecraft questions allow controlled knowledge cutoffs. Iterative retrieval reduces correct abstention in 30 of 40 configurations.
papers.key_insight: Evaluate retrieval depth separately from reliability. Track both accuracy on answerable questions and abstention when evidence is missing; a willingness to answer is not evidence coverage.

papers.title: Learning to Program Retrievals: Composing Search Primitives via Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Kyuyoung Kim, Zilin Xiao, Zhiyuan Wang, Avinash Atreya, Ke Yang, Jinwoo Shin, Kecheng Hao
papers.summary: Retrieval Program Learning trains a model to compose executable search programs and learn from constrained mutations of unsuccessful programs. Its 4B model averages 51.5% exact-match accuracy across seven QA benchmarks.
papers.key_insight: Separate retrieval breadth from context size: merge, deduplicate, and rerank locally, then expose only selected evidence. This allows broader evidence gathering without forcing the model to read every retrieved item.

papers.title: RemoteANN: A Native Vector Search Engine for Cloud Object Storage
papers.authors: Yutong Gou, Silu Huang, Yue Wang, Jianjun Chen, Cheng Long
papers.summary: RemoteANN co-designs vector indexing and query execution for cloud object storage. Quantized inverted lists, reordered data, merged range reads and local SSD caching reduce remote I/O. At matched target recall, the authors report up to 5.9× higher throughput than representative baselines.
papers.key_insight: The useful optimization target is remote requests per query. Data locality makes request merging and caching effective; faster distance computation alone cannot remove object-store latency.

papers.title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning
papers.authors: Liana Patel, Rishabh Ranjan, Ion Stoica, Matei Zaharia, Carlos Guestrin
papers.summary: TokenGate trains an existing model to skip less useful tokens in later layers. Token-gated attention supplies a learning signal for token selection. Across the tested tasks, the authors report up to 11.3× faster time to first token without measured accuracy loss.
papers.key_insight: Token selection can be learned during lightweight adaptation instead of imposed as a fixed heuristic. This targets prefill latency and memory, with an adaptation step required before deployment.

papers.title: E8-QAT: Efficient 2-Bit Quantization-Aware Training with Implicit Lattice Codebooks
papers.authors: Xinyu Lei, Hong Huang, Jiebin Zhang, Hongyu Li, Jinlong Song, Decheng Wu, Guanghua Yu, Jianchen Zhu, Sujian Li
papers.summary: Grouped weight quantization avoids an explicit codebook search by projecting onto a structured lattice. At each format’s largest feasible batch, decoding reaches 1.97 times BF16 throughput. This comparison includes the batch-size benefit of lower memory use.
papers.key_insight: Treat storage format and feasible batch size as coupled decisions. Arithmetic lattice projection reduces codebook search overhead, while memory savings create additional serving capacity.

papers.title: Large Flow Language Models
papers.authors: Arnav Chavan, Chanhyuk Lee, Udbhav Bamba, Jaehoon Yoo, Seunghoon Hong
papers.summary: Lafa adapts pretrained autoregressive models into blockwise continuous-flow language models. A single model proposes flow-based drafts and verifies them autoregressively, reaching 2.54 times autoregressive throughput at comparable quality.
papers.key_insight: Drafting and verification can share a model. Retaining autoregressive capability creates a verification path for parallel flow proposals without a separately maintained drafter.

papers.title: Is 2:4 Sparsity Still Worth It? Semi-Structured Sparsity versus Quantization in LLM Inference
papers.authors: Xiuyi Qin
papers.summary: An independent researcher compares "add 2:4 sparsity" versus "drop one precision tier" on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B under matched storage bits (including sparse indices) and matched nominal compute tiers, with measurements on L40S, H100, and RTX PRO 6000. ==As long as a lower precision is still available, adding 2:4 is both less accurate and slower==: 2:4 + INT8 costs the same storage as INT5. At the FP8 floor, a retrained 2:4 model served by vLLM on H100 raises prefill throughput 27% over dense FP8 with matched GSM8K; but ==during retraining perplexity recovers first while reasoning accuracy recovers much more slowly==.

deep_reading.content_html:
From Ampere onward, NVIDIA GPUs support 2:4 sparsity: in a matmul, one operand keeps 2 nonzeros per 4 elements along the accumulate axis, and tensor cores can nominally run twice as fast. It stacks with quantization, so the practical deployment question is: at the current precision, is the next step to add 2:4, or to drop one precision tier? This independent researcher's paper compares, on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B, under "matched storage bits (including sparse position indices)" and "matched nominal compute tiers," all six matmul operand roles in one transformer layer, with speed measured on L40S, H100, and RTX PRO 6000.
