Conclusion: as long as a lower precision tier is still available, adding 2:4 is both less accurate and slower; only at the hardware's lowest supported precision (FP8 on Ada/Hopper) does 2:4 pay off—on H100, a vLLM-served 2:4 + FP8 model raises prefill throughput 27% over dense FP8 with matched GSM8K, but only after retraining.

1. vLLM already removed 2:4 support—is it still worth using?

On one side every NVIDIA GPU generation keeps sparse tensor cores, and Blackwell adds sparse FP4; on the other, in 2026 vLLM and LLM Compressor removed 2:4 support for lack of users. Prior prune-versus-quantize comparisons mostly use "nominal compression," focus on weights, and do not put "add 2:4" versus "drop one precision" head-to-head on real hardware.

The authors flag four easy-to-miss points:

  • 2:4 stores a position index beside each kept value, so bits per original element exceed half;
  • both claim 2× throughput, but datasheets do not say how much you actually get;
  • at inference most operands (activations, Q, K, V, attention probabilities) are computed on the fly and must be pruned/compressed before every matmul—time invisible if you only time the matmul;
  • hardware dictates which operand may be sparse and along which axis, so tensor-wide statistics (e.g. kurtosis) do not show what 2:4 actually drops.

2. Method: compare at matched cost

2.1 Matched bits

Each format is billed by bits actually stored per original element—values, indices, and scales. Dense INTk uses one FP16 scale per 128 elements: $k+0.125$ bits/element; 2:4 keeps half the elements but adds 1 index bit per original element. So 2:4 + INT8 costs the same as dense INT5; 2:4 + INT4 equals INT3; 2:4 + FP16 costs more than FP8.

At matched storage the real choice is "drop half the elements and store the rest at 2× precision" versus "keep every element and add 1 bit each."

2.2 Matched compute tiers

Pair by datasheet nominal throughput: 2× tier is 2:4 + FP16 versus dense FP8/INT8; 4× tier is 2:4 + FP8 versus dense 4-bit float (Blackwell only).

2.3 How to measure

Accuracy is operator-level relative error versus an FP32 reference, summarized as $R=$ (best 2:4 config error) / (best quantization config error); $R<1$ means 2:4 wins. Each side picks the best among equally effortful methods: 2:4 tries magnitude pruning, Wanda, SparseGPT, etc.; quantization tries round-to-nearest, GPTQ, AWQ; all use C4 calibration. Speed uses cuSPARSELt sparse matmul; on-the-fly operands count online prune or online quantize time on both sides. Over 220K measured configs.

3. Experiments

3.1 Above the lowest precision: dropping a precision tier always wins

This checks whether adding 2:4 can ever be more accurate or faster while a lower precision is still available.

Accuracy. At matched bits, 2:4 loses at every storage budget on both models: at 8 bits the error gap is more than an order of magnitude; the gap shrinks as bits fall but does not vanish; under a 3.1-bit budget the closest comparison (Llama's K versus INT3) still has R slightly above 1. In the 2× tier, 2:4 + FP16 error is 5–16× dense FP8 on every operand.

Speed. Table below is "opponent time / 2:4 time"; >1 means 2:4 is faster (Llama-3.1-8B projection layers, median over 2K–16K tokens):

W = sparse weights, X = sparse activations (including online preprocess). Within each tier, the 2:4 side is slower. The authors' explanation: the energy in the 2 values 2:4 drops per 4 elements (sum of squares) cannot be recovered by giving the kept values more bits, while quantization error halves with each extra bit. On Gaussian data, elementwise 2:4 removes 13.2% of energy.

3.2 At the lowest precision: 2:4 can speed up, but needs retraining

This checks how much 2:4 helps at the FP8 or NVFP4 floor and at what cost. Linear-layer weights are 2:4; attention stays BF16; model is Llama-3.1-8B base.

vLLM end-to-end (single H100), 2:4 model = Sparse-Llama (2:4 Llama retrained on 13B tokens):

2:4 + FP8 beats dense FP8 on both prefill and decode, with no significant GSM8K difference. Serving the same weights with dense kernels removes the speedup, so the gain comes from sparse kernels. Under BF16, vLLM's 2:4 path is not faster than dense.

Retraining cost. One-shot pruning is unusable at every floor. Table: WikiText-2 perplexity / GSM8K accuracy (250 questions):

The authors retrain by distilling from the dense model on 1B FineWeb-Edu tokens: perplexity approaches Sparse-Llama, but GSM8K is only about half. Perplexity overestimates how much retraining has recovered; judging whether retraining is done requires reasoning tasks.

3.3 Blackwell sparse FP4

Blackwell sparse FP4 is not elementwise 2:4; it keeps 2 of 4 adjacent pairs per 8 elements. The kernel is 1.4× dense NVFP4, but removes 20.8% of energy on Gaussian data; one-shot pruning yields perplexity 108.83—five times elementwise 2:4; Sparse-Llama retrained for elementwise 2:4 cannot convert directly. Within the authors' 1B-token retrain budget, GSM8K recovers only to 0.132.

4. Limitations

Only two 8B models; Blackwell 4:8 conclusions are limited to 1B tokens and one untuned retrain recipe—whether longer retraining recovers is untested. The 4-bit integer weight floor (mainly for decode) has no speed numbers because vLLM removed the sparse kernels. Production often adds a Hadamard rotation before low-bit quantization; the authors note that makes 2:4 worse on most operands, so these unrotated results are optimistic for 2:4.

5. Takeaways

If the hardware still supports a lower precision (e.g. H100 BF16→FP8), drop precision first—do not add 2:4. If you already serve FP8, prefill throughput is the bottleneck, and you can get a fully retrained 2:4 model, 2:4 can give real speedups—but vLLM mainline removed support, so you must maintain it yourself. When evaluating a retrained sparse model, do not trust perplexity alone.

papers.title: Push-Based KV Transfer to Improve TTFT and TPOT for Disaggregated Inference in vLLM
papers.authors: Sunita Nadampalli; Nicolò Lucchesi
papers.summary: A push-based NIXL connector overlaps destination allocation with prefill and moves transfer setup off the decode loop. In the specified Qwen3-32B 1P1D test on EC2 P5en with EFA, TTFT improves by up to about 3× over pull mode.
papers.key_insight: Transfer ownership and setup placement matter alongside bandwidth. Overlap preparation with prefill and keep coordination off the token-generation critical path.

papers.title: Acceptance Is Not Speed: Length Inflation in Training-Free Lossy Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Chiatzen Wang, Bill Xu, Haochen Gu, Hongyang Zhang
papers.summary: Relaxed speculative verification can inflate completions enough to erase apparent decoding gains. Across matched prompts, the study tracks completion length, verifier rounds, runtime and accuracy. At the most relaxed settings, accepted tokens per round rise 1.34× while completions grow 1.54×.
papers.key_insight: Acceptance length is an incomplete speed metric when verification changes the output distribution. Track request completion time, output length and answer accuracy together; longer reasoning can consume the budget needed to return an answer.

papers.title: SGLang Low-Latency Mode: Kernels and Runtime
papers.summary: SGLang, NVIDIA, and AMD use a plugin framework to plug specialized fused kernels into SGLang, cutting inter-kernel waits and cross-GPU communication at low concurrency. On AgentX replays of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash + DSpark, per-user P90 generation rises from 671.2 to 928.4 token/s on 4×GB300 with 1 session, and from 331.6 to 516.0 token/s on 4×MI355X with 4 sessions. On NVIDIA, median time for one decode layer falls from 96.8 µs to 68.4 µs with almost the same kernel count; ==the speedup mainly comes from less waiting between kernels and overlapping work==.

deep_reading.content_html:
At low concurrency (for example an agent app with only one or two sessions per user), each request computes little data per step, and latency is spent on kernel launches, waits between kernels, and multi-GPU communication. SGLang, NVIDIA, and AMD describe SGLang's low-latency mode in this LMSYS blog: a plugin framework that plugs vendor-written, highly fused kernels for specific models and hardware into SGLang without merging that code into the SGLang main repo. The test model is DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with DSpark speculative decoding. On AgentX agent-trajectory replay, with 4 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs and 1 concurrent session, per-user P90 generation speed rises from 671.2 to 928.4 token/s (1.38×); with 4 AMD MI355X GPUs and 4 concurrent sessions, from 331.6 to 516.0 token/s (1.56×). Controls are standard SGLang on the same hardware.

1. Where time goes at small batch sizes

With one request, DSpark verifies only 6 token rows per step, so each kernel does little compute and dependencies plus cross-GPU communication dominate. Deep fusion for a specific model, hardware, and concurrency can cut latency a lot, but every combination needs its own implementation; putting them all in the SGLang main repo would keep growing code and review burden.

2. Method

2.1 NVIDIA: overlap dependent kernels and communication (sgl-nvidia-mega)

After warmup under a CUDA graph, the authors profile one decode layer (1 request, median per segment):

Kernel count only falls from 1,205 to 1,189; latency drops mainly by cutting waits and overlapping work, not by cutting kernel count. They do four things:

  1. Start the next kernel earlier. Using PDL (programmatic dependent launch, which lets a later kernel begin while an earlier one still runs), the "ready" signal is sent sooner so the next kernel can prepare barriers and load weights. Attention starts gathering KV before the query is ready; RoPE is done while loading the query, removing a separate kernel.
  2. Send results during the epilogue of the matmul. After the attention output projection each GPU holds a partial sum that must be reduced across GPUs. The baseline writes the matmul back to HBM and has the next kernel read it for the send; the plugin lets each thread block multicast over NVLink as soon as its tile finishes, without waiting for the whole matmul.
  3. Start expert matmuls before routing finishes. With at most 8 rows, tokens selected per expert fit in one 8-row tile; the plugin locates them with a bitmap and counts—no scan or sort—and starts the first expert matmul early. MoE median time falls from 44.4 µs to 36.5 µs.
  4. Pack speculative draft sampling into one kernel. DSpark's draft head proposes 5 tokens in order; the plugin finishes that on each GPU with one kernel launch, cutting draft time from 85.1 µs to 34.2 µs with the acceptance logic unchanged.

2.2 AMD: merge each layer into two resident kernels (sgl-amd-mono)

On AMD the authors see three large costs: even with HIP graphs each small kernel still costs 2–4 µs on the GPU; idle gaps between kernels; and no compute during two cross-GPU all-reduces per layer. The plugin uses FlyDSL to write two resident kernels covering most of a layer: K1 does mHC update, Q/KV projection, and KV-cache writes; K2 does attention, output projection, MoE, and both all-reduces. Stages pass "values tagged with the decode-step id"; matching ids start work without a separate flag. All-reduce is inside the kernel: each finished output tile is pushed to all GPUs while other workgroups keep computing. Each cross-GPU wait has a shorter timeout than the SGLang watchdog; on timeout all GPUs abort that launch instead of hanging the service.

2.3 Plugin framework

An external kernel library plugs in in four steps: register (declare supported model structures), check (before loading weights, verify hardware, precision, and parallelism, failing early on mismatch), build (prepare weights and resources at init, before KV-cache size is fixed so memory use is counted), and runtime dispatch (the plugin covers only some step types and token counts; uncovered steps fall back to SGLang's existing forward).

3. Experiments

3.1 AgentX trajectory replay

This measures how much the plugin speeds up a near-production agent load. Setup: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash + DSpark, TP4, per-user P90 generation speed, only the plugin switched.

On NVIDIA the speedup shrinks as concurrency rises; on AMD all three tiers stay above 1.45×.

3.2 NVIDIA fixed-length load

With 8K input and 1K output and a simulated mean acceptance length of 3.51, the NVIDIA plugin raises per-user decode speed by 12%–38% at 1–8 concurrent requests.

4. Limitations

Only DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash + DSpark is supported so far; GLM-5.3, K3, MiniMax M3 and others are still in development. The blog notes that profiling itself affects timing; per-segment numbers explain mechanisms, not serve as service SLOs. External kernels skip SGLang's usual code review; CI and performance regression for the plugin API are still planned; the API itself is early and will change. The blog gives no accuracy comparison and only states that speculative acceptance logic is unchanged.

5. Takeaways

If your load is low-concurrency and sensitive to per-user latency (for example coding or agent sessions) and you deploy DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on GB300 or MI355X, try this mode. For other models, the transferable pieces are the method: at small batches, profile waits and communication first, then decide which kernels to fuse; and isolate specialized kernels outside the main framework with plugins.

papers.title: llm-d 1.0, an open source stack for distributed inference
papers.authors: Google Cloud
papers.summary: Agent traffic is multi-step, shares long prefixes and arrives in bursts. Behind an ordinary round-robin load balancer, replicas recompute the same prompts and accelerator memory fills up with duplicate KV cache. llm-d 1.0, released at the PyTorch Conference by Google together with Red Hat, IBM and others, is an open-source distributed inference stack that runs on Kubernetes and organizes a set of vLLM and SGLang model servers into one serving pool: the router tracks which replicas hold each cached prefix and picks a replica using load and predicted latency; when accelerator memory fills up, KV cache is moved first to host memory and then to SSD; prefill and decode are split into two pools. Version 1.0 adds flow control that queues requests by priority and fairness, and rolling upgrades that do not interrupt sessions. On an agentic coding workload on Ironwood TPU, prefix-aware routing plus host-memory offload cut median time-to-first-token by more than 85% and delivered 2.4x the total throughput of a plain Kubernetes Service. ==The gain comes mainly from sending a session's requests back to the replica that already holds its context, which removes repeated prefill==.

deep_reading.content_html:
A year ago, most inference traffic was still chat: one prompt in, one response out. Now more and more requests come from multi-step agents and reinforcement-learning rollouts, which fan out across several tools, share very long prefixes and arrive in bursts. Put this traffic on a single machine, or behind an ordinary round-robin load balancer, and the replicas recompute the same prompts, accelerator memory fills up with duplicate KV cache, and one bursty agent loop can stall interactive users' requests. llm-d 1.0, released at the PyTorch Conference by Google together with Red Hat, IBM and others, is an open-source distributed inference stack that runs on Kubernetes and organizes a set of vLLM and SGLang model servers into one serving pool: the router knows which replicas hold each cached prefix and sends a session's requests back to them; when accelerator memory runs short, KV cache is moved to host memory and storage; high-priority requests can jump the queue. On an agentic coding workload on Ironwood TPU, prefix-aware routing plus host-memory offload cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by more than 85% and delivered 2.4x the total throughput of a plain Kubernetes Service. Most of these gains come from no longer recomputing prefixes that have already been computed, not from faster kernels.

This is a Google Cloud product blog, read together with IBM Research's introduction from the same day. Below, I first explain the problem llm-d solves, then break down four components, routing, KV-cache tiering, prefill/decode disaggregation and flow control, and finally look at the production numbers the blog gives. All numbers come from these two blogs, and most of them come without a full experimental setup.

1. The problem: why agent traffic breaks ordinary load balancing

LLM inference has two steps: prefill reads the whole prompt once and computes the KV cache for every token; decode then generates new tokens one by one from that cache. The compute of prefill grows with prompt length. An agent calls the model many times within one task, and every prompt contains the same system instructions, code and conversation history, with only a few new turns appended at the end.

If the second call is sent round-robin to a different replica, that replica has no cache from the first call and has to prefill the whole prefix again. The more replicas there are, the lower the chance of landing on the original one. IBM's blog puts it directly: if every step requires the model to reread the same material, you are repeatedly paying for work the system has already done.

The second problem is mixed load. Interactive requests need low latency, background agent loops and RL rollouts need throughput, and demand swings by the minute. Without priorities, interactive requests queue behind a large batch of background requests.

2. Method: four components

Cache-aware routing. The llm-d router is built on the Gateway API Inference extension for Kubernetes. It tracks which replicas hold each cached prefix and, when choosing a replica, weighs that information together with replica load and predicted latency. Version 1.0 adds session-aware routing and turn-priority scheduling, and stores Responses API state natively at the routing layer so agents can reuse context across turns. In IBM's words, multi-turn requests stay pinned to the appropriate replicas so that their prefix caches remain usable.

Tiered KV-cache offloading. Once accelerator memory is full, llm-d does not simply drop old cache; it uses vLLM's OffloadingConnector, Mooncake or SGLang's HiCache to move it to host memory, and further down to SSD or Google Cloud Managed Lustre. The point is to avoid many prefixes being pushed out of accelerator memory at once under multi-turn, long-context load and then recomputed all together; the blog calls this a prefix-eviction storm.

Prefill/decode disaggregation. Prefill is compute-heavy and decode is bound by memory bandwidth, so running both on the same replicas makes each wait on the other. llm-d splits prefill, decode and multimodal encode into separate pools, and uses wide expert parallelism to spread large MoE models across nodes. DisaggregatedSet, new in 1.0 and built on LeaderWorkerSet, the Kubernetes API for multi-host inference, manages these pools as one unit: during rolling updates, prefill and decode move together to matching versions, while scaling stays independent for each.

Flow control and async processing. Flow control queues requests by priority and fairness, so latency-sensitive requests and bursty agent workloads can share one set of hardware without starving each other. Version 1.0 also adds llm-d-async-processor, which pulls latency-tolerant requests from queues such as Pub/Sub or Redis, routes them alongside real-time traffic, runs them only on spare capacity, and enforces strict priority lanes and quotas.

This figure also shows where llm-d sits. It does not replace vLLM or SGLang; it sits in front of them and does the scheduling. Teams can keep their existing inference engine, models and cluster, and plug in only the components they need; the order the blog recommends is to first add prefix-aware routing in front of an existing vLLM deployment, then add flow control, KV-cache offloading and prefill/decode disaggregation.

3. What is new in 1.0

IBM's blog points out that the five techniques, prefix-cache-aware routing, KV-cache offloading, batch inference optimization, prefill/decode disaggregation and wide expert parallelism, existed before 1.0; what changes in 1.0 is that they can run long-term as a critical service. Specifically:

  • Multi-tenant quality of service: flow control by priority and fairness.
  • Stability: v1 APIs and a hardened request path, validated on multiple clouds and accelerator types.
  • Safer upgrades: router high availability, zero-downtime updates, and the DisaggregatedSet described above.
  • Agent-aware serving: session-aware routing, turn-priority scheduling and native Responses API state.
  • TPU support: TorchTPU runs PyTorch models natively on TPUs inside vLLM and SGLang, with cooperative time-slicing.

Time-slicing targets idle time in RL training. The blog says that during rollout generation or weight updates, accelerators sit idle 40% to 60% of the time; llm-d fits async inference into these gaps, raising aggregate accelerator duty cycles from a baseline of about 40% to more than 70%.

4. Experiments and production numbers

The blog's numbers fall into two kinds: Google's own tests and production traffic, and user reports. Each set gives only the comparison and the result, without a full experimental configuration; below they are organized by what they aim to show, what they compare against and the result.

ScenarioCompared againstResult
Agentic coding workload on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), prefix-aware routing + host-memory offloadPlain Kubernetes ServiceMedian TTFT down more than 85%, total throughput 2.4x
Gemini platform (formerly Vertex AI) production traffic through GKE Inference GatewayNot stated in the blogPrefix-cache hit rate from 35% to 70%; TTFT for coding agents down more than 35%; P95 TTFT under bursty chat traffic down more than 50%
17,000-node multi-region GKE deployment across the US and Europe serving an MoE modelNot stated in the blog (result is for three clusters combined)Throughput scaled 2.9x across three clusters, 99.9% success rate, routing overhead below 1%
A3 Mega cluster serving a 70B model, 50k-token prompts, KV cache offloaded to both Managed Lustre and host memoryOffload to host memory onlyTTFT improved about 40%, end-to-end latency down 30%, GPU-hour requirement down nearly 60%
Agentic coding workload test (IBM)Upper limit of reusable cachePrefix-aware router captured 97% of the available cache reuse
3,000 concurrent software-engineering agents, self-hosted deployment (IBM and Red Hat)Buying the same open model as a serviceCost 5 to 10 times lower

The first row answers how much cache-aware routing itself brings: on the same hardware, simply replacing round-robin with prefix-based routing and adding host-memory offload cut median TTFT by more than 85%. The second row is a check on production traffic: the prefix-cache hit rate doubled, consistent in direction with the drop in TTFT. The third row tests scale: routing overhead below 1% shows that the router's own computation did not become a bottleneck. The fourth row compares two KV-cache offloading schemes; with long 50k-token prompts, adding a shared storage tier has a clearer effect.

Among user reports, Snap reached prefix-cache hit rates of up to 75–80% with prefix-cache-aware routing; ZenteiQ raised daily generated tokens per 1,000 TPU v6e accelerators from 1.47 billion to 5.97 billion, more than 4x higher aggregate throughput; Mistral uses flow control to enforce strict priorities across its commercial tiers, automatically holding or shedding lower-priority requests when pools saturate.

5. Limitations

The blog itself does not discuss limitations. Two facts to add: first, most numbers in the table come with only a comparison and a result, so the baseline configuration, workload mix and measurement method need to be checked in the original sources linked from the blog; second, many capabilities (GKE Inference Gateway's managed routing, cross-region failover, the Managed Lustre storage tier) are Google Cloud managed services, and on other clouds or self-built clusters you need to deploy the corresponding open-source components yourself.

6. Practical takeaways

  • If you serve agents or multi-turn chat with vLLM or SGLang and still have round-robin load balancing in front, check the prefix-cache hit rate first. If it is low, prefix-based routing is the step with the smallest change and the most direct gain.
  • When interactive requests and batch jobs share the same GPUs, flow control and async queues let batch jobs use only spare capacity, so interactive latency is not affected by batch work.

papers.title: RCSD: Reinforcement and Continual Learning for Domain-Specific Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Mingkang Liu, Weiming Meng, Peipei Jiao, Jiawei Zhang, Tianyuan Liu, Junyan Li, Lichen Pang
papers.summary: Hisense's RCSD continues training a speculative-decoding draft model that was distilled with HASS, using DPO or GRPO: sequences from the target alone are "good," sequences alternating target and draft are "bad," and the GRPO variant scores by acceptance rate. On Qwen3-1.7B and Llama-3.1-8B, acceptance length exceeds HASS on four datasets and draft steps 3–6—for example Qwen3-1.7B on GSM8K at step 6 rises from 2.176 to 3.246, and Llama-3.1-8B ShareGPT throughput from 142.3 to 176.6 token/s. ==The paper reports no generation-quality evaluation==.

deep_reading.content_html:
Speculative decoding has a small draft model guess several tokens, then a large model verify them in one parallel pass; the more guesses accepted (longer acceptance length), the faster. Draft models are usually distilled so their output distribution matches the target, including low-probability tokens the target itself is unsure about. Hisense's authors argue that target is wrong: verification only cares whether the draft's tokens are accepted, so the draft only needs to rank the most likely few tokens correctly and need not reproduce the full distribution. They propose RCSD: in the EAGLE framework, start from a draft trained with HASS (a distillation method for draft models) and continue with DPO or GRPO, using contrast between sequences from the target alone and sequences that alternate target and draft. On Qwen3-1.7B and Llama-3.1-8B, acceptance length exceeds HASS on HumanEval, MT-Bench, GSM8K, and ShareGPT for draft steps 3–6; the paper reports a 35% average gain and 1.35× end-to-end speedup on ShareGPT-like loads.

1. Distillation target ≠ acceptance length

Distillation minimizes forward KL and forces the draft to spend capacity on every region of the target distribution, including the low-probability tail. The draft is orders of magnitude smaller and cannot fully match. The authors' claim: low KL need not mean high acceptance, and high KL can still accept well—what matters is whether the top few candidate tokens are ordered like the target.

2. Method

Both training variants start from a HASS-trained draft and keep it as a frozen reference.

DPO variant. For the same prompt, build a pair:

  • "Good" sequence: fully autoregressive from the target;
  • "Bad" sequence: the target emits 1 token, the draft continues for k tokens without verification, then repeat.

Standard DPO then raises the draft's probability of the good sequence relative to the reference and lowers the bad one. Tokens in the bad sequence that the target itself generated are masked out of the loss so the draft is not punished for matching the target.

GRPO variant. For the same prompt, generate a group: one sequence from the target alone, and several that alternate with different k (draft continues 1, 2, or 3 tokens). Each sequence's score is the sum of two normalized terms: the target's log probability of the sequence, and the sequence's acceptance rate. Train with GRPO's clipped objective plus a KL constraint.

3. Experiments

3.1 Acceptance length

This checks whether DPO/GRPO continued training makes more draft tokens accepted. Setup: Qwen3-1.7B and Llama-3.1-8B as targets, train on 90% of ShareGPT; test on HumanEval, MT-Bench, GSM8K, and the remaining 10% ShareGPT; draft steps 3–6.

Qwen3-1.7B at step 6 mean acceptance length; Llama-3.1-8B at step 6:

Both methods clearly beat HASS; GRPO is usually slightly better than DPO, with a small gap. Larger step sizes gain more—for example Qwen3-1.7B on GSM8K rises from +31% at step 3 to +49% at step 6. On Llama-3.1-8B the ShareGPT gain is largest, matching the training distribution.

3.2 Throughput

This checks whether longer acceptance becomes real speed. Setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, SGLang 5.5.0. The paper does not state the draft step for this plot; the acceptance lengths match the step-3 table above.

(token/s) On ShareGPT, GRPO rises from 142.3 to 176.6 token/s; the other three datasets gain less.

4. Limitations

  • The paper repeatedly claims "no quality impact" but gives no quality metrics. Speculative verification should make the target decide the output, but that is not separately checked.
  • The title mentions continual learning and domain-specific settings; the body has no continual-learning experiment and evaluates only general datasets.
  • Method text is inconsistent: Figure 3 left describes good/bad sequences from accepted versus early-rejected tokens, while the method section and the right panel use target-only versus target–draft alternating sequences.
  • Figure 2's caption says the baseline is SFT; the legend says HASS.
  • Throughput is measured only for one Llama-3.1-8B setup; training cost is unreported, and there is no comparison to non-distillation training methods.

5. Takeaways

If you already deploy an EAGLE/HASS-style draft, this paper suggests a low-cost next step: continue with one round of DPO on data from the target itself—no human labels or extra reward model. The GRPO variant is only slightly better and harder to implement. Without quality evals and training-cost numbers, check output consistency and training cost yourself before shipping.
